My relationship with my coworker Jasmine has changed a lot this year.
Few words passed between us early on - only talk of due dates. Then silence filled the gaps where conversation might have grown.
After that, our paths crossed again through a shared project. Working together became unavoidable once the assignments lined up.
Only later did I catch how her jokes land like dust settling - quiet, sharp, then gone.
These days, I usually get a coffee early, just before we all gather for work talk.
Frustration finds its way to her whenever my job spins out of control.
What stands out is how Jasmine tells the truth, straight, no smoothing edges. Her take hits hard sometimes, yet that’s exactly what makes it valuable.
Last week, right before the meeting, she stepped in when I was stuck on the slides. Five minutes left, and everything clicked because of her.
Just one person saw it happen.
Sometime soon, returning the gesture might make sense.
Perhaps pitch in on that analytics report - she said it was giving her trouble.
Friendships at work lighten the day, somehow. They turn tasks into moments that stick around longer than you’d expect.

Writing down some thoughts about my best friend Hannah.
We met freshman year in the college dorms.
Bonded immediately over late night pizza runs and complaining about chemistry class.
Ten years later she still knows me best.
When I moved to another state, she was the one who helped pack boxes.
Hannah has this calm way of listening when I’m stressed.
She rarely gives advice right away.
Instead she asks questions until I figure things out myself.
We try to do a video call every Sunday evening.
Sometimes we just talk about random shows we’re watching.
Other times we dive into serious life decisions.
I honestly can’t imagine life without her.
I need to book flights to visit her this summer.
She keeps inviting me to see the lake near her town.
Also bring the board games we used to play.
Traditions matter more than I thought.

Observations about my neighbor Carl across the hall.
We first met when he helped me carry a couch upstairs.
These days, our talks by the lockers happen more than once in a while.
Carl is retired from the postal service.
He takes that familiar path each dawn, circling the neighborhood streets without change.
Most folks around here? He can call them by their first name.
Frost still heavy on the ground, he cleared the path alone while the house stayed quiet. Quietly, snow fell again just after dawn. The street remained empty until long past sunrise.
It's things like these that give the place its warm touch.
Beneath the lamp light, he recalls slipping through icy streets with letters tucked under his coat.
Finding him happens most while I carry the trash outside.
Every time we talk, he wants to know about my progress looking for work.
Folks living close by, chatting now and then, make things feel different. A word here, a laugh there - suddenly it matters.
Perhaps offer a coffee meet-up one day.
